title: Books burned (Acts 19:1–20)
hook: new believers in Ephesus burn their magic scrolls
tomorrow: a whole city shouts one line for two hours. who finally stops it?

segments.voice: That was a week on the road with Paul: a split and a mending, a riverbank, songs at midnight, a town that checked, an altar with no name, and a couple who corrected kindly. Yesterday's line: more perfectly.

Deleting an app you paid for is strangely hard. You keep thinking about what it cost, and what you might be missing. In Ephesus, people carry their scrolls out into the open, books of what the King James calls curious arts, magic, and burn them where everyone can watch. Why would new believers set fire to their own books? It starts with a failed exorcism, and a spirit that talks back.
screen: `HARD TO DELETE WHAT YOU PAID FOR.` → `SCROLLS INTO THE OPEN.` → `A SPIRIT THAT TALKS BACK.`

segments.voice: Paul has been teaching in Ephesus daily, in the school of a man named Tyrannus, and Acts says God worked special miracles by his hands. Some traveling exorcists, seven sons of a man named Sceva, try Jesus' name like a borrowed key. The evil spirit answers, "Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?" and the man it holds leaps on them, and they run from the house wounded. The name was never a spell to borrow. Word gets around, and the city shifts. "Many that believed came, and confessed, and shewed their deeds." Then the fire: "Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men: and they counted the price of them, and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver." They don't sell the scrolls to someone else. They don't keep one back. And here's the one to tell a friend: Acts doesn't hide the cost, it counts it. Then a single line: "So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed." Notice the order. Confessing first, then the fire, then the growing.
screen: `BUT WHO ARE YE?` · `CONFESSED, AND SHEWED THEIR DEEDS.` · `THEY COUNTED THE PRICE.` · `SO MIGHTILY GREW THE WORD.` · then, large: `THE WORD GREW.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing within reach that keeps pulling you somewhere you'd rather not go: an app, a tab, an object on the desk. Do one small thing about it now: move it off your home screen, close it, or put it in a drawer. It doesn't have to be forever; it only has to be real. If you pray, you can bring it before God by name.
Books burned. Scrolls of curious arts, carried out and burned before all men in Ephesus, their price counted.
The line for today: the word grew, after the confessing and after the fire. Week done.

howItsDone: Christians read Acts 19 as a picture of turning from old ways; some, preparing for baptism or confession, name and set aside things they mean to leave behind.

fork.setup: your cousin is quitting a phone game that's been eating her sleep. her account has rare items worth real money, and she plans to sell it to a friend. what fits Ephesus?
options: let it go entirely, even though it costs her.
sell it; at least the money goes somewhere useful.
keep the account, just in case she misses it.
fork.reveal: they didn't sell the scrolls or keep one back. Acts counts the cost, and lets it burn.

chat.says: left the gossip group chat kayla runs. feels weird and quiet. too dramatic?
options: Not dramatic. In Ephesus people cleared out what kept pulling them down, even at a cost. It counts.
A bit. The Ephesus believers kept their books and simply stopped reading them. No big move.
Only if you announce it. They burned the books in public to prove everyone else wrong.
chat.meaning: In Ephesus, believers confessed and burned what had a hold on them, counting the cost. Clearing something out isn't drama; it's room for growth.

Ephesus.meaning: a large city on the coast of Asia where Paul taught

Sceva.meaning: a man whose seven sons tried to drive out a spirit

curious arts.meaning: the King James phrase for magic practices
